summary: This Best Current Practice gives guidelines for operating authoritative servers, recursive resolvers, and stub resolvers in mixed IPv4/IPv6 environments. It recommends both authoritative and recursive servers support both protocols, and advises how resolvers choose upstream servers. It obsoletes RFC 3901.

eli5.summary: A phone book must answer calls from both old and new phone lines, and this tells it how to pick.

subtitle: How to keep DNS working when some networks speak only IPv4 and others only IPv6.

tldr.problem: The Internet still mixes IPv4-only, dual-stack and IPv6-only networks, so a resolver can hit a zone whose name servers it cannot reach with its own address family, and the DNS is effectively split in two.
tldr.mechanism: Zones must be served by at least two IPv4-reachable and two IPv6-reachable name servers with consistent data and no fragmentation reliance, recursive resolvers SHOULD be dual-stack, and stub resolvers follow address selection rules and a limit on how many resolvers they are given.
tldr.outcome: This Best Current Practice obsoletes RFC 3901, which focused on IPv4 continuity, and now recommends IPv6 alongside IPv4 for authoritative servers, recursive resolvers and stub resolvers.

today: RFC 10001 is a Best Current Practice published in August 2026. It obsoletes RFC 3901 and is not itself marked as obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs Mixed-Network Guidance
sections.content:
RFC 10001 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 91) for running authoritative servers, recursive resolvers and stub resolvers in a mixed IPv4/IPv6 Internet. It obsoletes RFC 3901.

The Internet still consists of IPv4-only, dual-stack and IPv6-only networks. A resolver may reach the Internet over only one address family, yet it can receive queries for names whose authoritative servers sit on the other one.

RFC 3901 was written when IPv6 was not widely deployed and focused on name space continuity inside the IPv4 landscape. This document broadens the scope by recommending IPv6 connectivity for all three kinds of DNS component. Making DNS data reachable over both IPv4 and IPv6 is called the most robust and flexible approach, because it avoids translation or encapsulation services that can add failure cases.
sections.eli5: Some roads are old and some are new, and a delivery truck may only fit on one kind. This document says to build both roads to every house so nothing gets stuck.

sections.title: Terms and Definitions
sections.content:
The document builds on the DNS terminology of RFC 9499 and defines a few terms of its own.

  • IPv4-reachable name server: serves authoritative or recursive DNS over IPv4. This says nothing about the data it serves.
  • IPv6-reachable name server: the same, over IPv6.
  • Dual-stack name server (or resolver): both IPv4-reachable and IPv6-reachable.
  • Effective PMTU: the largest IP packet, in octets, that can cross a path without fragmentation.

The usual BCP 14 requirement words apply when they appear in capitals.
sections.eli5: Before giving advice, the document names the kinds of helpers: ones that answer on the old road, ones on the new road, and ones on both.

sections.title: Name Space Partitioning
sections.content:
A resolver starts at the root and follows referrals until it reaches the name servers for a name. If those servers are reachable only over an address family the resolver does not support, resolution stops. The DNS is then partitioned for that resolver.

The RFC sorts the causes into three groups.

  • Misconfigurations: NS names with only A or only AAAA records, missing IPv4 or IPv6 glue in the parent, missing A or AAAA records for in-domain NS names in the child, sibling-domain NS names whose own zone does not resolve over that family, or a parent zone that is not resolvable over that family. Any of these may also be an address record for a server that does not actually answer on that family. They can stay hidden because dual-stack clients fall back to the other family.
  • Network conditions: mainly silent MTU discards of packets that would need fragmentation, plus broken IP connectivity at the resolver.
  • Intentional choices: an operator deliberately leaves out A or AAAA records for NS names. A 2023 study cited by the RFC found the share of zones not resolvable via IPv4 negligible, while a little less than 40% of zones were not resolvable via IPv6.
sections.eli5: If a letter can only be delivered by a road that the mail carrier cannot drive on, it never arrives. That can happen by mistake, because of bad roads, or because someone chose it.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Path MTU Problems
sections.content:
Packets that exceed the path MTU may be dropped silently, so a resolver just times out. The RFC covers both transports.

DNS over UDP. Servers SHOULD follow RFC 9715, which suggests an upper bound of 1400 octets for received EDNS(0) sizes. The DNS Flag Day 2020 initiative suggests 1232 octets, which keeps packets within 1280 octets, the minimum IPv6 MTU. The RFC notes that clients MAY use an EDNS(0) size of 1232 octets as well.

DNS over TCP. Path MTU Discovery can fail when ICMP messages are dropped or altered, and it costs time that DNS often cannot spare. Servers SHOULD therefore configure the maximum response size, for TCP by limiting the MSS. It is RECOMMENDED that servers set a sender MSS of no more than 1388 octets, giving packets of at most 1448 octets. Servers MAY use 1220 octets to stay within 1280.

As an extra precaution, servers MAY decline to rely on PMTUD or PLPMTUD, for example by setting IPV6_USE_MIN_MTU=1. Other transports such as DNS-over-TLS or DNS-over-QUIC should use any anti-fragmentation measures they have, and otherwise follow the TCP and UDP guidance by analogy.
sections.eli5: A big parcel might get stuck in a narrow tunnel, so the advice is to pack smaller parcels and keep a backup way to send them.

sections.title: Rules for Authoritative Servers
sections.content:
To prevent partitioning, at least two IPv4-reachable and two IPv6-reachable name servers MUST be configured for a zone. One server reachable over both families counts once per family. All names used in NS records are RECOMMENDED to have both an A and an AAAA record set, so resolvers do not waste queries on NODATA answers.

The key requirements are:

  • IPv4: at least two servers over IPv4, and NS delegation (parent resolution, sibling names, glue) MUST NOT rely on IPv6.
  • IPv6: at least two servers over IPv6, no IPv4-embedded addresses (including IPv4-mapped) for receiving queries, and delegation MUST NOT rely on IPv4.
  • Consistency: both transports MUST serve equivalent DNS data.
  • Avoiding fragmentation: follow RFC 9715, and DNS-over-TCP MUST be available as a fallback, as per RFC 7766. Servers MAY set an MSS of 1388 or 1220 on TCP sessions.

Zone validation SHOULD check that child delegations have at least two IPv4 and two IPv6 address records for their name servers, that servers follow RFC 9715, support DNS-over-TCP, and are reachable over each family from IPv4-only and IPv6-only networks.
sections.eli5: Every phone book must have at least two helpers on the old line and two on the new line, all giving the same answers, and a backup way to send big answers.

sections.title: Rules for Recursive and Stub Resolvers
sections.content:
Every recursive resolver SHOULD be dual-stack. Exceptions exist when another method prevents partitioning. A recursive resolver MAY be IPv6-only if it uses a transition mechanism to reach IPv4-only servers, or forwards failed queries to a dual-stack recursive resolver. If it knows a PREF64 for NAT64, it MAY synthesize IPv6 addresses for remote authoritative servers. An IPv4-only resolver MAY likewise forward failed queries to a dual-stack one. Answers to recursive queries SHOULD follow the same fragmentation-avoidance guidance as above.

Stub resolvers usually run on end hosts, and learn recursive resolver addresses from DHCPv4, DHCPv6 or router advertisements. They SHOULD follow RFC 6724 to prioritize addresses, and SHOULD NOT use IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses if they can recognize them, for example by knowing the PREF64.

Some implementations accept only a few resolver addresses, for example up to three for glibc. When offering more than three, operators SHOULD either use one address family only, or give exactly two addresses of one family and exactly one of the other. All supplied resolvers SHOULD be able to do dual-stack resolution.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle should know both roads. Your own device should pick the best helper from its list, and should not be given so many helpers that it forgets some.

sections.title: Security and Operational Cautions
sections.content:
The guidelines add no new security considerations to the DNS protocol itself, but the RFC describes corner cases.

An infinite forwarding loop can arise when two resolvers each support only one, different address family, each forwards queries it cannot handle to the other, and a query arrives for a zone that is resolvable over neither family. To prevent it, single-stack resolvers SHOULD forward to dual-stack resolvers, and recursive resolvers MUST NOT forward to resolvers that forward to them.

An incorrect PREF64 can cause security issues, so guidance from RFC 9872 on securely discovering it SHOULD be followed. Avoiding fragmentation can raise load through more TCP fallbacks. Measurements put this at 3-5% of connections, and operators SHOULD monitor the impact. There are no IANA actions, though IANA should consider requiring both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses for each authoritative server.
sections.eli5: If two helpers keep passing a question back and forth because neither can answer it, it never ends. So helpers must not pass questions in a circle.
